readings.c1s1:
¶
'''awane''' (a̤-wān′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''wane''.] On the wane; waning.

'''awanting''' (a̤-wân′ting), ''a.'' [Prop. a phrase, ''a wanting''; cf. ''amissing''.] Wanting; deficient; absent; missing: not used attributively.
{{smaller block|In either case criticism was required, and criticism was ''awanting''.
{{right|''Sir W. Hamilton.''}}}}

'''awape†''', ''v. t.'' See ''awhape''.

'''award'''<sup>1</sup> (a̤-wârd′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''awarden'', < AF. ''awarder'', OF. ''eswarder'', ''eswardeir'', later ''esgarder'', ''esguarder'', ''esgardeir'' = Sp. ''esguardar'' (obs.) = It. ''sguardare'', look at, consider, decide, adjudge, < ML. *''exwardare'', < L. ''ex'', out, + ML. ''wardare'', ''guardare'', observe, regard, guard: see ''ward'', ''guard'', and ''regard''.] '''1.''' To adjudge to be due; assign or bestow as of right; give by judicial determination or deliberate judgment, especially upon arbitration or umpirage: as, to ''award'' the prizes at a school examination; the arbitrators ''awarded'' him heavy damages.
{{smaller block|<poem>A pound of that same merchant’s flesh is thine:
The court ''awards'' it, and the law doth give it.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iv. 1.}}
To the woman who could conquer, a triumph was ''awarded''. ''Marg. Fuller'', Woman in 19th Cent., p. 47.}}
'''2†.''' To sentence; adjudge or determine the doom of.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lest . . . the supreme King of kings . . . ''award''
Either of you to be the other’s end.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 1.}}
<poem>                The extremity of law
''Awards'' you to be branded in the front.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, v. 1.}}}}
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''awater''' (ạ-wâ′tėr), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''water.''] On the water.

'''awave''' (ạ-wāv′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''wave.''] On the wave; waving.

'''away''' (ạ-wā′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ME. ''away'', ''awey'', ''awei'', ''oway'', ''o wey'', ''on way'', etc., < AS. ''aweg'', earlier ''on weg'', lit. on way: see ''a''<sup>3</sup> and ''way.''] '''1.''' On the way; onward; on; along: as, come ''away''.
{{smaller block|Mistress, you must come ''away'' to your father.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' From this or that place; off: as, to go, run, flee, or sail ''away''.
{{smaller block|He rose and ran ''away''. ''Shak.'', Pass. Pilgrim, iv. 14.
<poem>And we kiss’d the fringe of his beard and we pray’d as we heard him pray,
And the Holy man he assoil’d us, and sadly we sail’d ''away''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Voyage of Maeldune.}}}}
'''3.''' From one’s own or accustomed place; absent: as, he is ''away'' from home; I found him ''away'' on a vacation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thyself ''away'' art present still with me;
For thou not farther than my thoughts canst move.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, xlvii.}}}}
'''4.''' From contact or adherence; off: as, to clear ''away'' obstructions; cut ''away'' the broken spars.
{{smaller block|<poem>Before the golden tresses of the dead
. . . were shorn ''away''. ''Shak.'', Sonnets, lxviii.</poem>}}
'''5.''' Removed; apart; remote: as, ''away'' from the subject.
{{smaller block|<poem>Quite ''away'' from aught vulgar and extern.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 122.}}}}
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''6.''' From one’s possession or keeping: as, to give ''away'' one’s books or money; throw ''away'' a worn-out or discarded thing.
{{smaller block|<poem>O there, perchance, when all our wars are done,
The brand Excalibur will be cast ''away''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}}

'''7.''' From one’s immediate presence, attention, or use; aside: as, put or lay ''away'' your work; put ''away'' your fears; the things were laid ''away'' for the summer.
{{smaller block|<poem>Put ''away''
These dispositions, which of late transport you
From what you rightly are.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4.}}}}

'''8.''' From this or that direction; in another or the other direction: as, turn your eyes ''away;'' he turned ''away''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Often, where clear-stemm’d platans guard
The outlet, did I turn ''away''
The boat-head down a broad canal.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Arabian Nights.}}}}

'''9.''' At or to such a distance; distant; off: as, the village is six miles ''away''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Mirthful sayings, children of the place,
That have no meaning half a league ''away''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}
An hour ''away'', I pulled up, and stood for some time at the edge of a meadow.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Trans. Sketches, p. 136.}}}}

'''10.''' From one state or condition to another; out of existence; to an end; to nothing: as, to pass, wear, waste, fade, pine, or die ''away;'' continual dropping wears ''away'' stone; the image soon faded ''away;'' the wind died ''away'' at sunset; she pined ''away'' with consumption.
readings.c3s3:
terrify; control or restrain by the influence of fear.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor think thou with wind
Of aery threats to ''awe'' whom yet with deeds
Thou canst not.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 283.}}
<poem>Never be it said
That fate itself could ''awe'' the soul of Richard.</poem>
{{right|''Cibber'', Rich. III., v. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' To strike with awe, reverence, or respect; influence by exciting profound respect or reverential fear.

'''awe<sup>2</sup>''' (â), ''v. t.'' [Sc., = E. ''owe.''] To owe. [Scotch.]

'''awe<sup>3</sup>''' (â), ''n.'' [Sc. also ''ave'', early mod. E. also ''aw'', ''aue'', ''ave'', ''alve''; origin obscure.] '''1.''' One of the float-boards of an undershot water-wheel, on which the water acts.—'''2.''' One of the sails of a windmill.

'''aweary''' (ạ-wēr′i), ''a.'' [< ''a-'' expletive + ''weary.''] Weary; tired. [Archaic or poetical.]
{{smaller block|<poem>She said, “I am ''aweary'', ''aweary'',
I would that I were dead!”</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Mariana.}}
And all his people told him that their horses were ''aweary'', and that they were ''aweary'' themselves.
{{right|''Ticknor'', Span. Lit., I. 66.}}}}

'''aweather''' (ạ-weᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''weäther.''] On the weather side, or toward the wind: as, the helm is ''aweather'': opposed to ''alee.''

'''aweel''' (ạ-wēl′), ''adv.'' [Sc., < ''a'' for ''ah'', oh, + ''weel'' = E. ''well.''] Oh well; very well; well then.
{{smaller block|''Aweel'', if your honour thinks I’m safe—the story is just this.
{{right|''Scott'', Guy Mannering, II. 63.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>                The extremity of law

{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, v. 1.}}}} '''3.''' In a general sense, to permit the possession of; allow; allot; yield.
{{smaller block|The child had many more luxuries and indulgences than had been ''awarded'' to his father.
{{right|''Thackeray.''}}}}

'''award<sup>1</sup>''' (a-wârd′), ''n.''   [< ME. ''award'', < AF. ''award'', OF. ''eswart'', ''esguart''; from the verb.]   '''1.''' A decision after examination and deliberation; a judicial sentence; especially, the decision of arbitrators on points submitted to them, or the document containing such a decision.
{{smaller block|We cannot expect an equitable ''award'' where the judge is made a party.
{{right|''Glanville.''}}}}
'''2.''' That which is awarded or assigned by such a decision, as a medal for merit, or a sum of money as damages, etc.—{{smaller|'''Geneva award.''' See ''Alabama claims'', under ''claim''.}}

'''award<sup>2</sup>†''', ''v. t.''   [< ''a-''<sup>11</sup> + ''ward''.]   '''1.''' To guard. —'''2.''' To ward off.   ''Evelyn.''

'''awarder''' (a-wâr′dėr), ''n.'' One who awards or assigns as of right; a judge, arbitrator, or umpire.

'''aware''' (a-wãr′), ''a.''   [< ME. ''aware'', ''iwar'', ''iware'', ''ywar'', < AS. ''gewǣr'' (= OHG. ''giwar'', MHG. ''gewar'', G. ''gewahr''), < ''ge-'' + ''wǣr'', wary, cautious: see ''a-''<sup>6</sup>, ''ge-'', and ''ware''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' Watchful; vigilant; on one’s guard.
{{smaller block|I have laid a snare for thee, and thou art also taken, O Babylon, and thou wast not ''aware''.
{{right|Jer. l. 24.}}}}
{{smaller block|Are you all ''aware'' of . . . tale-bearing and evil-speaking?
{{right|''Wesley'', Works (1872), XIII. 19. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
'''2.''' Apprised; cognizant; in possession of information: as, he was ''aware'' of the enemy’s designs. {{smaller block|I was so distinctly made ''aware'' of the presence of something kindred to me . . . that I thought no place could ever be strange to me again. {{right|''Thoreau'', Walden, p. 143.}}}}
Specifically—'''3.''' Informed by sight or other sense.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then Enid was ''aware'' of three tall knights
On horseback, wholly arm’d, behind a rock,
In shadow, waiting. {{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}</poem>}}
='''Syn. 2.''' ''Aware'', ''Conscious'' (see ''conscious''), mindful, acquainted (with), sensible, observant.

'''awareness''' (a̤-wãr′nes), ''n.'' The state of being aware.
{{smaller block|Recognition of reality in our view is not ''awareness''. {{right|''Mind'', X. 525.}}}}
{{smaller block|This consciousness I speak of is not a direct perception of the Absolute, but a general ''awareness'' that it exists. {{right|''New Princeton Rev.'', II. 178.}}}}

'''awarn†''' (a̤-wârn′), ''v. t.''   [< ''a-'' + ''warn''.]   To warn.
{{smaller block|<poem>Every bird and beast ''awarned'' made
To shrowd themselves. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. x. 46.}}</poem>}}

'''awash''' (a̤-wosh′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''a.'' or ''adv.''   [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''wash''.]   ''Naut.'': (''a'') Just level with or emerging from the surface of the water, so that the waves break over it, as wreckage, or an anchor when hove up to the surface, or rock, spit, or bank just appearing above the water.
{{smaller block|The wrecks are floating almost ''awash'', presenting little surface for the wind to blow upon. {{right|''Science'', III. 363.}}}}
(''b'') Covered with water; kept wet: as, the decks were constantly ''awash''. (''c'') Washing about; tossed about by the waves.

'''awaste''' (a̤-wāst′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''   [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''waste''.]   Wasting; going to waste or decay.

'''Awata ware, pottery.''' See ''ware''.

'''awater''' (ạ-wâ′tėr), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''   [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''water.'']   On the water.

'''awave''' (ạ-wāv′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''   [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''wave.'']   On the wave; waving.

'''away''' (ạ-wā′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''   [< ME. ''away'', ''awey'', ''awei'', ''oway'', ''o wey'', ''on way'', etc., < AS. ''aweg'', earlier ''on weg'', lit. on way: see ''a''<sup>3</sup> and ''way.'']   '''1.''' On the way; onward; on; along: as, come ''away''.
{{smaller block|Mistress, you must come ''away'' to your father.
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' From this or that place; off: as, to go, run, flee, or sail ''away''.

{{right|''Tennyson'', Voyage of Maeldune.}}}}

{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, II. 122.}}}}

'''6.''' From one’s possession or keeping: as, to give ''away'' one’s books or money; throw ''away'' a worn-out or discarded thing.
{{smaller block|<poem>O there, perchance, when all our wars are done,

{{smaller block|<poem>Put ''away''
These dispositions, which of late transport you

'''8.''' From this or that direction; in another or the other direction: as, turn your eyes ''away;'' he turned ''away''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Often, where clear-stemm’d platans guard
The outlet, did I turn ''away''
The boat-head down a broad canal.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Arabian Nights.}}}}

'''9.''' At or to such a distance; distant; off: as, the village is six miles ''away''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Mirthful sayings, children of the place,
That have no meaning half a league ''away''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}}
{{smaller block|An hour ''away'', I pulled up, and stood for some time at the edge of a meadow.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Trans. Sketches, p. 136.}}}}

'''10.''' From one state or condition to another; out of existence; to an end; to nothing: as, to pass, wear, waste, fade, pine, or die ''away;'' continual dropping wears ''away'' stone; the image soon faded ''away;'' the wind died ''away'' at sunset; she pined ''away'' with consumption.

{{smaller block|The new philosophy represented by Locke, in its confidence and pride taking a parting look at the old philosophy, represented by the scholastic discussions, passing ''away'' in the midst of weakness and ridicule.
{{right|''McCosh'', Locke’s Theory of Knowledge, p. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|Without adducing one fact, without taking the trouble to perplex the question by one sophism, he [Mr. Mill] placidly dogmatises ''away'' the interest of one half of the human race.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Mill on Government.}}}}
'''11.''' Gone; vanished; departed: as, here’s a health to them that’s ''away''. [Chiefly prov. Eng. and Scotch.]—'''12.''' On; continuously; steadily; without interruption: as, he worked ''away;'' he kept pegging ''away;'' and hence often as an intensive: as, to fire ''away'', eat ''away'', laugh ''away'', snore ''away''.
{{smaller block|As if all the chimneys in Great Britain had, by one consent, caught fire and were blazing ''away'' to their dear hearts’ content.
{{right|''Dickens''.}}}}
'''13.''' Often used elliptically, with a verb (as ''go'', ''get'') suppressed, and simulating an imperative: as, (go) ''away!'' (get) ''away!'' we must ''away;'' whither ''away'' so fast?
{{smaller block|''Away'', old man! give me thy hand, ''away!''
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|Love hath wings, and will ''away''.
{{right|''Waller''.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Away'', ''away'', there is no danger in him.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, v. 4.}}}}

'''Away back''', {{smaller|far back; long ago: as, ''away back'' in the years before the war; ''away back'' in 1844. [Colloq. often '''way back''.]}}—'''Away with.''' {{smaller|(''a'') Used as an imperative phrase, commanding the removal of an object.}}
{{smaller block|''Away with'' this man, and release unto us Barabbas.
{{right|Luke xxiii. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Away with'' you! . . . I’ll put everybody under an arrest that stays to listen to her. {{right|''Sheridan'', The Camp, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') An elliptical expression for “get away with,” that is, get on with; accommodate one’s self to; endure. [Archaic.]}}
{{smaller block|Some agayne affirme that he retorned into his countrey, but partly for that he coulde not ''away with'' the fashions of his countrey folk, and partly for that his minde and affection was altogether set and fixed upon Utopia, they say that he hathe taken his voyage thetherwarde agayne. {{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (Arber), p. 165.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Shal.'' She never could ''away with'' me.

''Fal.'' Never, never; she would always say she could not abide Master Shallow. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|I could never ''away with'' that stiff-necked generation. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Bartholomew Fair, i. 1.}}}}
'''Far away, far and away.''' {{smaller|(''a'') At a great distance. (''b'') By far. [Colloq.]}}
{{smaller block|Of all the men whom she had ever seen, he was ''far away'' the nicest and best. {{right|''Trollope.''}}}}
'''Right away,''' {{smaller|straightway; at once; immediately; forthwith.}}—'''Say away,''' {{smaller|say on; proceed with your remarks. [U. S. and prov. Eng.]}}—'''To bear away, explain away, fire away, make away,''' {{smaller|etc. See the verbs.}}—'''To make away with.''' {{smaller|See ''make.''}}

'''away-going''' (a-wā′gō″ing), ''a.'' and ''n.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Going away; departing; leaving: as, an ''away-going'' tenant.—'''Away-going crops,''' {{smaller|crops sown during the last year of a tenancy, but not ripe until after the expiration of it.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A going away; departure.

'''awaywward†''' (a-wā′wärd), ''adv.''   [ME., also ''aweiward'', etc.; < ''away'' + ''-ward''.]   Turned aside.   ''Gower.''

'''awbert†''', ''n.''   [< F. ''aubour'', OF. ''aubour'', also ''aubourt'' (Cotgrave), laburnum, appar. < L. ''alburnum'': see ''alburnum'' and ''laburnum''.]   The laburnum-tree, ''Cytisus Laburnum''.   ''Increase Mather'', Remark. Provid., p. 232. (''N. E. D.'')

'''awe<sup>1</sup>''' (â), ''n.''   [Also, more prop., ''aw'' (like ''law'', ''haw'', etc.), < ME. ''aw'', ''awe'', ''agh'', ''aghe'', ''aȝe'', < Icel. ''agi'' = Dan. ''ave'' = AS. as if *''aga'', the same with diff. formative as AS. ''ege'', ME. ''eȝe'', ''eghe'', ''eye'', ''aye'', ''ay'', = OHG. ''agi'', ''egi'', MHG. ''ege'' = Goth. ''agis'', fear, < *''agan'', fear (in ppr. *''agands'', with negative ''unagands'', unfearing); perhaps akin to Gr. ἄχος, anguish. Cf. ''ask''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' Dread; fear, as of something evil.
{{smaller block|<poem>I had as lief not be as live to be
In ''awe'' of such a thing as I myself.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|In every form of government, the rulers stand in some ''awe'' of the people. {{right|''Macaulay'', Mill on Government.}}}}
'''2.''' Fear mingled with admiration or reverence; reverential fear; feeling inspired by something sublime, not necessarily partaking of the nature of fear or dread.
{{smaller block|Stand in ''awe'', and sin not. {{right|Ps. iv. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|The [Egyptian] deities representing the great forces of nature, and shrouded by mysterious symbols, excited a degree of ''awe'' which no other ancient religion approached.
{{right|''Lecky'', Europ. Morals, I. 345.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To feel once more, in placid ''awe'',
The strong imagination roll
A sphere of stars about my soul,
In all her motion one with law.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, cxxii.}}}}
'''3.''' Overawing influence.
{{smaller block|By my sceptre’s ''awe'' I make a vow.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., i. 1.}}}}
='''Syn.''' ''Reverence'', ''Veneration'', etc. See ''reverence'', ''n.''

'''awe<sup>1</sup>''' (â), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''awed'', ppr. ''awing''.   [< ''awe''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''1.''' To inspire with fear or dread; terrify; control or restrain by the influence of fear.
{{smaller block|<poem>Nor think thou with wind
Of aery threats to ''awe'' whom yet with deeds
Thou canst not.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vi. 283.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Never be it said

{{right|''Cibber'', Rich. III., v. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|<poem>She said, “I am ''aweary'', ''aweary'',
I would that I were dead!”</poem>
